To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the performance of Monte Carlo neutron transport simulations can be greatly increased by using the Intel Many Integrated Core (MIC) architecture, and that the performance of such simulations can be increased by a factor of 5.6 by using the new algorithm that calculates the cross sections on the fly.

we have developed an efficient method to calculate the cross sections on the fly, and that we have developed a new method to access cross sections from a database, which is based on an optimized binary search.
we have demonstrated that the performance of MCNP5 can be significantly enhanced by using a novel approach that calculates cross sections on the fly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimization of Monte Carlo neutron transport simulations on many-core architectures.
the development of new algorithms for MC neutron transport simulations that can exploit the capabilities of modern many-core platforms.
the optimization of Monte Carlo neutron transport simulations on many core architectures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the work done in the thesis has been to propose a solution to the memory latency problem in MCNP, which is to replace the data look-up tables by a calculation of the data at the fly.
, for this particular case, a hybrid approach, where some data are pre-computed and cached and others are computed on-the-fly, is the best option.

the work presented in this thesis has allowed to demonstrate that, in terms of performances, the best solution is to use the pre-computed cross sections in memory and to optimize the code in a way to take full profit of the many cores of the MIC architecture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a new method to compute cross sections on the fly.
we have shown how to efficiently implement a Monte Carlo neutron transport code on a many-core processor, by using a combination of memory optimization, data-driven algorithms, and parallelization.
we have developed a new approach for the calculation of the nuclear data needed for Monte Carlo simulations, which can significantly improve the overall performance of these simulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the memory latency is the main bottleneck in Monte Carlo simulations.

it is possible to obtain significant speedups for Monte Carlo neutron transport codes by taking advantage of the many-core architectures and the specificities of the MIC architecture (vectorization and multithreading).
the memory-boundness of the MC algorithm is not necessarily a problem for the many-core architectures, as long as the data is available in cache memory.
